sentences.t:
Unferð maþelode, Ecglāfes bearn,
þē æt fōtum sæt frēan Scyldinga,
onband beadurūne —
sentences.l: Unferth spoke in speech-words, Ecglaf's child, who at the feet sat of the lord of the Scyldings, unbound battle-rune —
sentences.i: Unferth spoke in formal words, the son of Ecglaf, who sat at the feet of the Scyldings' lord, and let slip his quarrelsome thoughts —
sentences.n: ‘Unferð maþelode’ uses the speech-introducing verb of the house rows (past of ‘maþelian’), and ‘Ecglāfes bearn’, ‘Ecglaf's child’, is in apposition to the name, with ‘Ecglāfes’ in the genitive. In ‘þē æt fōtum sæt’ the ‘þē’ is the relative ‘who’ (usually written ‘þe’), and ‘fōtum’ is dative plural after ‘æt’: ‘at the feet of’ the king, ‘frēan Scyldinga’, genitive plural ‘of the Scyldings’ (‘frēan’ itself is the dative singular of ‘frēa’, ‘lord’, after ‘æt’ with ‘fōtum’). To sit at a ruler's feet was presumably a place near him, but the poem does not say what office it implies. The verb is ‘onband’, past of ‘onbindan’, ‘unbind’, and its object is ‘beadurūne’, an accusative singular, ‘battle-rune’: ‘rūn’ is a secret, a whispered counsel (the word behind ‘rune’), so ‘unbound battle-rune’ is ‘let loose a hostile secret’, or ‘opened his quarrel’; I take the unbinding as the opening of something held in. The name is a problem in the manuscript. The apparatus gives the manuscript's name here as ‘HVN ferð’, that is ‘Hunferð’, and Klaeber prints ‘Unferð’; the italic ‘Un’ is his sign that he changed those letters. Rieger proposed this form because the line alliterates on vowels (‘Unferð’, ‘Ecglāfes’), and the apparatus suggests that the scribe confused the name with names beginning ‘Hūn-’. The same change is made at line 530. If ‘un-’ here is the negative prefix, the name could mean something like ‘un-peace’ (‘ferð’ would then be a guess for ‘frið’); that is only a guess.

sentences.t:
wæs him Bēowulfes sīð,
mōdges merefaran, micel æfþunca,
forþon þe hē ne ūþe, þæt ǣnig ōðer man
ǣfre mǣrða þon mā middangeardes
gehēde under heofenum þonne hē sylfa —:
sentences.l: was to him Beowulf's venture, the bold sea-farer's, a great grudge, because he did not grant that any other man ever of glories more of middle-yard should heed under the heavens than he himself —:
sentences.i: — for Beowulf's voyage, that bold seafarer's, was a great vexation to him, since he would not grant that any other man should ever win or keep more glory in the world under heaven than he himself —:
sentences.n: The dash at the end of the previous unit opens a parenthesis, and this unit gives the reason for Unferth's hostility; the dash at the end closes it, and the colon opens the speech. ‘wæs him Bēowulfes sīð … micel æfþunca’ is ‘was to him Beowulf's venture a great grudge’: ‘him’ is dative, ‘sīð’ (a going, a venture) is the subject, ‘Bēowulfes’ is genitive and ‘mōdges merefaran’, ‘of the bold sea-farer’, is a second genitive in apposition. ‘æfþunca’ is ‘grudge, envy’ (‘æf-’ is ‘off, away’ and ‘þunca’ is ‘thought’; the compound is a guess at the exact shade, but all the aids agree on envy or vexation). ‘forþon þe’ means ‘because’. ‘ne ūþe’ is the past of ‘unnan’, ‘to grant, allow’, followed by a ‘þæt’-clause with its verb in the subjunctive, ‘gehēde’: ‘he did not grant that any other man should …’. ‘mǣrða’ is the genitive plural of ‘mǣrþu’, ‘glories’, and ‘middangeardes’ (‘middle-yard’, the world, as in the middle region between heaven and hell) is a second genitive, so ‘glories of the world’; ‘þon mā … þonne’ is ‘more … than’. ‘gehēde’ needs a word about the text. The manuscript has ‘gehedde’; Holthausen's ‘gehēde’ has a single ‘d’, and Klaeber's italic ‘d’ marks it as changed. The apparatus points to Sievers and to Klaeber's own textual section but does not give the reason, so I cannot say whether it is metrical or grammatical. The verb ‘gehēdan’ (‘take heed of, take care of’, hence ‘hold, win’) is a guess at the shade; the sense of jealous rivalry for fame is clear from ‘ne ūþe’. The envy is the point: Unferth cannot bear a rival, and Beowulf's reply at 532–534 turns the same wording (‘ǣnig ōþer man’) back on him.

sentences.t:
‘Eart þū sē Bēowulf, sē þe wið Brecan wunne,
on sīdne sǣ ymb sund flite,
sentences.l: ‘Art you that Beowulf, that one who against Breca strove, on the wide sea about swimming in contest,
sentences.i: ‘Are you that Beowulf who strove against Breca, contending in a swimming-match on the wide sea,
sentences.n: A question with the verb first: ‘Eart þū’, ‘art you’, second person singular of ‘wesan’. ‘sē Bēowulf, sē þe …’ is ‘that Beowulf, he who …’, with ‘sē’ the demonstrative used like ‘that famous’; the verb of the relative clause, ‘wunne’, is a past subjunctive, which I take to be the mood of a thing reported rather than vouched for (a guess at the force): Unferth does not say he saw it. ‘wið Brecan’ puts the dative after ‘wið’, ‘against Breca’ (a weak noun in the dative). ‘on sīdne sǣ’ is ‘on the wide sea’, with ‘sīdne’ an accusative masculine (‘sǣ’ can be masculine or feminine), and ‘ymb sund flite’ is ‘about swimming in contest’: ‘flite’ is the dative of ‘flit’, ‘strife, contest’, the same word that gives the later English ‘flyting’, a contest of insults, which is exactly what this scene is. ‘Breca’ is introduced without explanation, so the audience knew the tale; we learn only from Unferth's own lines (521) that he is lord of the Brondings.

sentences.t:
ðǣr git for wlence wada cunnedon
ond for dolgilpe on dēop wæter
aldrum nēþdon?
sentences.l: where you two, out of pride, the waters tried, and for folly-boast in deep water risked your lives?
sentences.i: where, out of pride, the two of you tried the waters, and for a foolish boast risked your lives in the deep?
sentences.n: Here is the dual. Old English had separate pronouns for exactly two people: ‘wit’ ‘we two’, ‘git’ ‘you two’, with the accusative and dative ‘unc’ ‘us two’ and ‘inc’ ‘you two’. Unferth uses ‘git’ for Beowulf and Breca, and Beowulf will answer with ‘wit’ and ‘unc’; these notes translate them ‘you two’, ‘we two’, ‘us two’. ‘ðǣr’ is ‘where’. ‘for wlence’ is ‘out of pride’ (‘wlenc’, pride, high spirits, dative), and ‘for dolgilpe’ is ‘for folly-boast’, a compound of ‘dol’, foolish, and ‘gilp’, boast (related to ‘yelp’; the sense is a vain boast). ‘wada cunnedon’ is ‘tried the waters’; ‘cunnian’ (‘try, test’) takes the genitive or the accusative, and ‘wada’ is probably the plural of ‘wæd’, ‘water, sea, shallows’ (cf. ‘wado’, 546), though the exact case is a guess. ‘aldrum nēþdon’ is ‘risked their lives’: ‘aldrum’ is dative plural of ‘aldor’, ‘life’, and ‘nēþan’ means ‘to venture’. Unferth's charge is vanity and bravado, not courage, and Beowulf will repeat his words ‘aldrum nēðdon’ at 538 to take the venture back.

sentences.l: Nor you two could any man, neither dear nor loathed, dissuade from the sorrow-full venture, when you two onto the water rowed;
sentences.i: Nor could any man, friend or foe, dissuade you two from that sorrowful venture when you struck out upon the water;
sentences.n: ‘Nē inc ǣnig mon … belēan mihte’ is ‘not you two any man could dissuade’: ‘inc’ is the dual accusative, ‘belēan’ has ‘inc’ and ‘sorhfullne sīð’ as its objects (‘dissuade you two from the venture’; the aids give ‘blame, forbid, dissuade’, and I take the last), and ‘mihte’ is a past form, probably subjunctive after a negative (the past singular indicative and subjunctive of ‘magan’ can look alike). ‘nē lēof nē lāð’ is ‘neither dear nor loathed’, an old formula for ‘nobody, whoever he was’ (friend or enemy; cf. ‘lief’). ‘sorhfullne sīð’ is ‘sorrow-full venture’ with both words accusative masculine singular, and it means a venture that ended in grief, as Unferth intends it. ‘reôn’ is a contracted form (Klaeber's circumflex) of ‘rēowon’, the past plural of ‘rōwan’, ‘to row’, here used of the swimmers' stroke; whether it means that they swam with their arms or really rowed something is not said, and ‘rowed’ in the literal line is chosen for that reason.

sentences.l: where you two the water-stream with arms covered, measured the sea-streets, with hands moved, glided over the gar-secg;
sentences.i: where you two covered the stream of the sea with your arms, measured out the sea-roads, swung your hands, and glided over the ocean;
sentences.n: A run of four past plurals with ‘git’ understood as the subject of each: ‘þehton’ (from ‘þeccan’, ‘cover’), ‘mǣton’ (from ‘metan’, ‘measure’), ‘brugdon’ (from ‘bregdan’, ‘move quickly, pull, swing’) and ‘glidon’ (from ‘glīdan’, ‘glide’). The datives ‘earmum’ and ‘mundum’ are instrumental, ‘with arms’, ‘with hands’. The three sea-words are of three kinds. ‘ēagorstrēam’ is ‘water-stream’, and ‘ēagor’ is a poetic word for water or sea that occurs very rarely (it may be related to the English dialect word ‘eagre’, a tidal bore, but that is a guess). ‘merestrǣta’ is a kenning: ‘mere’ is the sea and ‘strǣt’, from Latin ‘strata’, is a paved road, the origin of ‘street’; ‘measured the sea-streets’ means ‘covered the sea-roads’. ‘gārsecg’ is the old word for the ocean; its literal sense is perhaps ‘spear-man’ (‘gār’ spear, ‘secg’ man), but the meaning ‘ocean’ is secure and the origin is unknown, so ‘l’ keeps the Old English. The sea is a road and the swimmers measure it, which makes the swim sound grand in Unferth's telling.

sentences.t:
geofon ȳþum wēol,
wintrys wylm[um].
sentences.l: the flood with waves welled, with winter's surges.
sentences.i: the flood surged with waves, with the swells of winter.
sentences.n: A short clause with the verb ‘wēol’ (past of ‘weallan’, ‘well up, seethe’) and ‘geofon’, a neuter noun for the sea or flood, as subject; ‘ȳþum’ is a dative plural of manner, ‘with waves’. ‘wintrys’ is a genitive singular of ‘winter’ (the usual form is ‘wintres’; ‘-ys’ is a variant spelling), so ‘winter's surges’, which tells us the season of the swim. The bracketed ending in ‘wylm[um]’ is Klaeber's addition. The manuscript has only ‘wylm’, and the apparatus lists four ways to mend it: Thorkelin, Rieger, Sievers, Schücking and Chambers add ‘-e’ (‘wylm[e]’, dative singular, ‘with the surge’); Möller, Holthausen and Sedgefield add ‘[þurh]’ before it (‘through the surge’); and Kluge's ‘wylm[um]’, dative plural ‘with surges’, which Klaeber prints, with a parallel at Andreas 451 f. The sense is the same in all of them. ‘wylm’ is the noun from the same root as the verb ‘weallan’, so the line says twice over that the water is boiling.

sentences.t:
Git on wæteres ǣht
seofon niht swuncon;
sentences.l: You two in the water's keeping seven nights toiled;
sentences.i: The two of you toiled seven nights in the water's grip;
sentences.n: ‘Git … swuncon’ is the dual subject and the past plural of ‘swincan’, ‘toil’ (our ‘swink’). ‘on wæteres ǣht’ is ‘in the water's possession’: ‘ǣht’ (also ‘āht’) is ‘possession, power’, here a power that holds them, and ‘wæteres’ is genitive. ‘seofon niht’ is an accusative of duration, ‘for seven nights’, with ‘niht’ unchanged in the plural. Time was counted in nights by the Germanic peoples, which survives in ‘fortnight’ and ‘sennight’. Seven is Unferth's count; Beowulf's own is five at 545, and the poem leaves the difference unexplained.

sentences.t:
hē þē æt sunde oferflāt,
hæfde māre mægen.
sentences.l: he you at swimming out-strove, had more strength.
sentences.i: He outdid you at swimming, for he had the greater strength.
sentences.n: Two short statements side by side, with no word for ‘because’ (a feature of Old English, which joins by juxtaposition): ‘hē þē æt sunde oferflāt’ and ‘hæfde māre mægen’. ‘hē’ is Breca and ‘þē’ is the dative ‘you’. ‘oferflāt’ is the past singular of ‘oferflītan’, ‘overcome in a contest’ (the same root as ‘flite’ at 507), so ‘out-strove’; ‘æt sunde’ is ‘at swimming’, dative. ‘māre mægen’ is ‘more strength’, ‘māre’ the comparative accusative of ‘micel’. Unferth gives his verdict in two short clauses and no detail.

sentences.t:
Þā hine on morgentīd
on Heaþo-Rǣmas holm ūp ætbær;
sentences.l: Then him at morning-time to the Heathoreams the sea up bore;
sentences.i: Then at morning the sea carried him up to the Heathoreams;
sentences.n: ‘Þā hine … holm ūp ætbær’: ‘hine’ is Breca, accusative, and the subject is ‘holm’, the sea (or a wave), a masculine noun; ‘ætbær’ is the past of ‘ætberan’, ‘carry to’, here with ‘ūp’, ‘up’, so the sea bore him up and delivered him. ‘on morgentīd’ is ‘at morning-time’. ‘Heaþo-Rǣmas’ is a people-name that Klaeber prints with an italic ‘a’, and the apparatus explains it. The manuscript reads ‘heaþoræmes’; Klaeber changes the ending ‘-es’ (the italic ‘a’) to ‘-as’, the ending that an accusative plural after ‘on’ needs. The vowel is a second question: Munch, Müller, Holthausen, Schücking and Sedgefield read ‘-Rēamas’ and Grein and Chambers read ‘-Rǣmas’, as Klaeber does. The passage does not say who the Rǣmas are. I recall the name being linked with the Raumar of the Norse sources, but that is memory, not something in the aids, so treat it as unverified. The first element ‘Heaþo-’ (‘battle’) may be an epithet; that is a guess too. Klaeber's capital letters, the hyphen and the vowel length are his, not the manuscript's.

sentences.t:
ðonon hē gesōhte swǣsne ēþel,
lēof his lēodum, lond Brondinga,
freoðoburh fægere, þǣr hē folc āhte,
burh ond bēagas.
sentences.l: thence he sought his own homeland, dear to his people, the land of the Brondings, the peace-borough, fair, where he folk owned, borough and rings.
sentences.i: From there he made for his own country, dear to his people, the land of the Brondings, the fair stronghold where he ruled over a people, town and treasure.
sentences.n: A single sweep of apposition, with ‘swǣsne ēþel’ (accusative, ‘his own homeland’) glossed by ‘lond Brondinga’ (‘land of the Brondings’, genitive plural) and by ‘freoðoburh’, ‘peace-borough’, a fortified place that gives ‘freoðu’, protection (‘fægere’ is most likely the accusative feminine of ‘fæger’, ‘fair’, though an adverb ‘fairly’ is also possible). ‘lēof his lēodum’ is ‘dear to his people’, dative plural. ‘ðonon’ is ‘thence’, and ‘gesōhte’ is the past of ‘gesēcan’, ‘seek out, reach’. The relative clause ‘þǣr hē folc āhte, burh ond bēagas’ says what he owned: ‘āhte’ (past of ‘āgan’, ‘own’) governs ‘folc’, ‘burh’ and ‘bēagas’, ‘folk, borough and rings’, and ‘rings’ stand for the treasure a lord gives out. So the account of the swim ends with Breca as a lord with a country and a following. ‘ēþel’ needs a note: the manuscript does not write the word out, but uses a single rune-letter that is also called ‘ēþel’ (apparatus: ‘MS. [ēþel rune]’; likewise at 913 and 1702), and Klaeber prints the word.

sentences.t:
Bēot eal wið þē
sunu Bēanstānes sōðe gelǣste.
sentences.l: Boast all against you the son of Beanstan truly fulfilled.
sentences.i: Beanstan's son made good the whole of his boast against you, truly.
sentences.n: The object comes first: ‘Bēot eal … gelǣste’ is ‘fulfilled the whole vow’. ‘bēot’ is the formal vow or boast the warrior makes in public, ‘eal’ is ‘all’, ‘wið þē’ is ‘against you’, ‘sōðe’ is ‘truly’ and ‘gelǣste’ is the past of ‘gelǣstan’, ‘carry out, perform’. ‘sunu Bēanstānes’ is ‘son of Beanstan’, the genitive of a name otherwise unknown. The apparatus offers two alternatives, ‘Bānstānes’ (Bugge, with a query, and Krüger) and ‘Bēahstānes’ (Bugge, with a query), but Klaeber keeps ‘Bēanstānes’. ‘Bēan-’ looks like the word for ‘bean’, an odd element for a name, so the sense of the name is a guess; the doubtful alternatives would mean ‘bone-stone’ (‘bān’) and ‘ring-stone’ (‘bēah’). Unferth says Breca carried out his whole boast; which boast he means is not said, though Beowulf is about to describe a vow the two made as boys.

sentences.t:
Ðonne wēne ic tō þē wyrsan geþingea,
ðēah þū heaðorǣsa gehwǣr dohte,
grimre gūðe, gif þū Grendles dearst
nihtlongne fyrst neân bīdan.’
sentences.l: Then expect I of you a worse outcome, though you in battle-rushes everywhere availed, in grim war, if you of Grendel dare a night-long space near await.’
sentences.i: So I look for a worse result from you, though you have proved good in every battle-rush, in grim war, if you dare to wait for Grendel nearby for the space of one night.’
sentences.n: ‘Ðonne’ here is ‘then, in that case’, and the sentence has two conditions, one conceded (‘ðēah … dohte’) and one open (‘gif … dearst’). ‘wēne ic tō þē’ is ‘I expect from you’ (‘wēnan’, ‘expect’). The object ‘wyrsan geþingea’ is a crux. ‘wyrsan’ is ‘worse’, but ‘geþingea’ has an ending that fits no noun I can identify with confidence; ‘geþinge’ is ‘agreement, outcome, terms’. The apparatus lists Kemble's ‘þinges’ (with a query) and Rieger's and Sedgefield's ‘geþinges’, a genitive after ‘wēnan’, which would give ‘a worse outcome’; I render ‘a worse outcome’ and mark it as a guess. ‘dohte’ is a past subjunctive of ‘dugan’, ‘avail, be good’ (cf. ‘doughty’), concessive after ‘ðēah’: ‘though you were good’. ‘heaðorǣsa gehwǣr’ is ‘everywhere in battle-rushes’ (‘rǣs’ is a rush, an onset; ‘heaðorǣsa’ is genitive plural, and ‘gehwǣr’ is ‘everywhere’), and ‘grimre gūðe’ is ‘in grim war’, dative. In the last clause ‘dearst’ is the second person singular of ‘durran’, ‘dare’, ‘Grendles’ is a genitive after ‘bīdan’ (‘bīdan’, ‘wait for’, takes a genitive), ‘neân’ is a contracted ‘from near’, and ‘nihtlongne fyrst’ is an accusative of time, ‘for a night-long space’. The closing quotation mark is Klaeber's.

sentences.t: Bēowulf maþelode, bearn Ecgþēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: The same pattern as the speech-introduction at 499, with the verb ‘maþelode’ first after the name (house row, as at 286 and 371), and the epithet ‘bearn Ecgþēowes’, ‘child of Ecgtheow’, appositive to the name and with ‘Ecgþēowes’ genitive. Ecgþēow is Beowulf's father, who is named at 263 and whose feud was the subject of Hrothgar's speech in the previous fitt. The two introductions answer each other: one man ‘unbinds’ a hostile speech, the other answers in the same formal verb.

sentences.t:
‘Hwæt, þū worn fela, wine mīn Unferð,
bēore druncen ymb Brecan sprǣce,
sægdest from his sīðe!
sentences.l: ‘What! You a great many things, friend mine Unferth, drunk with beer, about Breca in talk, said of his venture!
sentences.i: ‘Listen! You have said a great deal about Breca in your talk, my friend Unferth, drunk with beer, and told of his voyage!
sentences.n: ‘Hwæt’ is the house opening, ‘What!’ in the literal line and ‘Listen!’ in the idiomatic. The one finite verb is ‘sægdest’ (second person singular past of ‘secgan’, ‘say’), and its object is ‘worn fela’, ‘a great many’ (‘worn’ is a multitude, and ‘fela’ is ‘many’; together they are ‘a great deal’) in the accusative. ‘sprǣce’ I take as the dative singular of the noun ‘sprǣc’, ‘speech, talk’, so ‘ymb Brecan sprǣce’ is ‘about Breca, in talk’; it could also be read as a second verb, ‘you spoke’, but two finite verbs side by side with no ‘and’ is unlikely, and none of the lexical aids I am allowed to use settles it for this line, so the reading is a judgment, not a certainty. ‘from his sīðe’ (‘of his venture’, dative) goes with ‘sægdest’. ‘wine mīn Unferð’ is a vocative: Hrothgar called Beowulf ‘wine mīn Bēowulf’ at 457, and Beowulf now gives the phrase back with a barb. ‘bēore druncen’, ‘drunk with beer’ (‘druncen’ the past participle, ‘bēore’ the dative of the thing), is a plain insult and it prepares the point of Beowulf's story: what Unferth said was beer-talk. The name ‘Unferð’ has the same problem as at 499: the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘hun ferð’, here too reduced to ‘Unferð’ by Klaeber (italic ‘Un’), and refers back to 499.

sentences.t:
Sōð ic talige,
þæt ic merestrengo māran āhte,
earfeþo on ȳþum, ðonne ǣnig ōþer man.
sentences.l: Sooth I reckon, that I sea-strength greater owned, hardships on the waves, than any other man.
sentences.i: I reckon it the truth that I had more sea-strength, and endured more hardships on the waves, than any other man.
sentences.n: ‘Sōð ic talige’ is ‘truth I reckon’: ‘talige’ is the first person singular of ‘talian’, ‘count, reckon, claim’ (cf. ‘tell’, ‘tale’), and ‘sōð’ is its object, ‘the truth’. The ‘þæt’-clause has ‘āhte’, a past subjunctive of ‘āgan’, ‘own, have’, with two objects, ‘merestrengo māran’ (‘greater sea-strength’; ‘merestrengo’ is a feminine accusative) and ‘earfeþo on ȳþum’ (‘hardships on the waves’). The second is uncertain: Heyne's glossary (?), Bugge and Trautmann read ‘eafeþo’, ‘strength’, instead of ‘earfeþo’, and the apparatus adds ‘See 577’, a cross-reference I have not followed up. With ‘eafeþo’ the two objects would both be strength; with Klaeber's ‘earfeþo’ the second is hardships, and Beowulf is claiming both strength and suffering. I follow Klaeber. ‘ðonne ǣnig ōþer man’ is ‘than any other man’, and it picks up Unferth's grudge at 503–505 (‘ǣnig ōðer man … þonne hē sylfa’): Beowulf now makes the claim that Unferth could not bear anyone else to make.

sentences.t:
Wit þæt gecwǣdon cnihtwesende
ond gebēotedon —
sentences.l: We two that agreed, being boys, and vowed —
sentences.i: As boys we two agreed on it, and vowed —
sentences.n: ‘Wit’ is the dual ‘we two’ (see 508), the subject of ‘gecwǣdon’ (past plural of ‘gecweþan’, ‘say, agree’) and ‘gebēotedon’ (past plural of ‘gebēotian’, ‘make a vow’, from ‘bēot’, 523). ‘þæt’ looks forward to the content clause in 537. ‘cnihtwesende’ is the present participle of ‘wesan’ with ‘cniht’, ‘boy’, ‘being boys’, in the nominative plural in apposition to ‘wit’. The dash opens a parenthesis, which the next unit closes.

sentences.t:
wǣron bēgen þā gīt
on geogoðfēore —
sentences.l: were both then yet in youth-life —
sentences.i: — we were both still in the days of youth —
sentences.n: The parenthesis. ‘wǣron bēgen þā gīt’ is ‘were both then yet’, with ‘bēgen’ the masculine nominative ‘both’ and ‘þā gīt’ ‘still at that time’; do not confuse ‘gīt’ (‘yet’, with a long vowel) with the dual pronoun ‘git’. ‘on geogoðfēore’ is ‘in youth-life’, a dative: ‘fēore’ is the dative of ‘feorh’, ‘life’, and ‘geogoð’ is ‘youth’. Beowulf stresses that they were boys.

sentences.t:
þæt wit on gārsecg ūt
aldrum nēðdon, ond þæt geæfndon swā.
sentences.l: that we two on the ocean out risked our lives, and that accomplished so.
sentences.i: that we would risk our lives out on the ocean; and so we did.
sentences.n: The content of the vow: ‘þæt wit on gārsecg ūt aldrum nēðdon’ is ‘that we two would venture our lives out onto the ocean’, with the past plural ‘nēðdon’ of ‘nēðan’ as in Unferth's own line 510 (spelled ‘nēþdon’ there), and with the same dative ‘aldrum’; Beowulf takes Unferth's phrase and shows it was meant as a vow, not folly. ‘ond þæt geæfndon swā’ is ‘and that we carried out so’: ‘geæfndon’ is the past plural of ‘geæfnan’, ‘perform, accomplish’, and ‘swā’ ‘so, in that way’. The two verbs have no subject word because ‘wit’ is carried over.

sentences.t:
Hæfdon swurd nacod, þā wit on sund reôn,
heard on handa;
sentences.l: We had swords naked, when we two onto the water rowed, hard in hand;
sentences.i: We had naked swords in hand, hard and ready, when we struck out onto the water;
sentences.n: ‘Hæfdon’ is a past plural with ‘wit’ understood from before (‘we had’), and ‘swurd nacod’ is ‘naked sword’: ‘nacod’ is ‘naked’, that is drawn, out of its scabbard. The ‘þā’-clause repeats Unferth's ‘on sund reôn’ (512), so Beowulf is re-using the words Unferth used. ‘heard on handa’ is ‘hard in hand’; ‘handa’ is a dative (the older -a ending), and ‘heard’ most naturally agrees with the swords: ‘hard’, that is ‘firm, ready, not to be put down’. It could also describe the swimmers' grip, which is a guess I cannot settle. Unferth's story had no swords in it; this detail makes the swim a matter of fighting sea-creatures.

sentences.t:
wit unc wið hronfixas
werian þōhton.
sentences.l: we two ourselves against whale-fishes to defend thought.
sentences.i: we two meant to defend ourselves against the whale-fishes.
sentences.n: ‘wit unc … werian þōhton’ is ‘we two intended to defend ourselves two’: ‘unc’ is the dual reflexive accusative, ‘werian’ is ‘defend’ (the root of ‘ward’, ‘weir’), and ‘þōhton’ is the past plural of ‘þencan’, ‘think, intend’. ‘wið hronfixas’ is ‘against whale-fishes’ (‘hron’, whale; ‘fisc’, fish; ‘-fixas’ is ‘-fiscas’ with the ‘s’ and ‘c’ swapped (metathesis, which other Old English words show too)). The apparatus reports that Schücking proposed ‘hornfiscas’, ‘horn-fishes’ (with a parallel at Andreas 370), but also cites ‘hronfiscas’ from the Old English Epistola Alexandri (510), so the manuscript form stands. The ‘whale-fishes’ are probably sea-monsters in general, which is a guess; ‘merefixa’ (549) is the same idea in a word of its own.

sentences.t:
Nō hē wiht fram mē
flōdȳþum feor flēotan meahte,
hraþor on holme, nō ic fram him wolde.
sentences.l: Not he at all from me on the flood-waves far to swim could, faster on the sea, nor I from him would.
sentences.i: He could not at all swim far from me over the flood-waves, nor faster on the sea; nor would I leave him.
sentences.n: ‘Nō … wiht’ is ‘not at all’ (‘wiht’, a thing, used adverbially; cf. ‘aught’ and ‘naught’). ‘hē’ is Breca and ‘fram mē’ is ‘from me’. The infinitive ‘flēotan’ means ‘float, swim’; ‘flōdȳþum’ is a dative plural of place or means, ‘on the flood-waves’; ‘feor’ is ‘far’ and ‘hraþor’ (the comparative of ‘hraþe’, ‘quickly’) is ‘more quickly’; ‘on holme’ is ‘on the sea’, dative. Together the clause says that Breca could neither get far from Beowulf nor beat him for speed, which answers Unferth's ‘oferflāt’ at 517 directly. The second half has no verb of motion: ‘nō ic fram him wolde’ is ‘nor would I from him’, with ‘wolde’ a past subjunctive that carries the verb forward from ‘flēotan’. This is a boast that they were evenly matched, not that Beowulf won.

sentences.t:
Ðā wit ætsomne on sǣ wǣron
fīf nihta fyrst, oþ þæt unc flōd tōdrāf,
wado weallende, wedera cealdost,
nīpende niht, ond norþanwind
heaðogrim ondhwearf;
sentences.l: Then we two together on the sea were five nights' space, until the flood drove us two apart, the waters welling, coldest of weathers, darkening night, and the north-wind, battle-grim, turned against us;
sentences.i: Then we two were together on the sea for the space of five nights, until the flood drove us apart, the waters surging, the coldest of weathers, the night closing in, and the north wind, grim as battle, turned upon us;
sentences.n: A long sentence with a clear skeleton: ‘wit … wǣron fīf nihta fyrst’ (‘we were five nights' space’; ‘fyrst’ is ‘space of time’, here an accusative of duration like ‘nihtlongne fyrst’ at 528, with ‘nihta’ a genitive plural), ‘oþ þæt unc flōd tōdrāf’ (‘until the flood drove us two apart’, with ‘unc’ the dual accusative and ‘tōdrāf’ the past of ‘tōdrīfan’), and ‘norþanwind … ondhwearf’ (‘the north wind turned against us’). In between come three phrases that set the scene, loosely joined to the clause: ‘wado weallende’ (‘waters welling’; ‘wado’ is a plural, probably of ‘wæd’ as at 508), ‘wedera cealdost’ (‘coldest of weathers’, genitive plural, partitive) and ‘nīpende niht’ (‘darkening night’, a present participle of ‘nīpan’, ‘grow dark’); then the wind, with ‘heaðogrim’ (‘battle-grim’) an adjective on it. ‘ondhwearf’ is a manuscript problem. The apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘⁊ hwearf’, that is ‘ond hwearf’ with the Tironian sign for ‘and’; Grein read ‘and hwearf’ with ‘hwearf’ as an adjective (the apparatus compares Finnsburg 34), and Trautmann and Holthausen read ‘onhwearf’. Klaeber joins the two into one verb, ‘ondhwearf’ (‘ond-’ being a form of the prefix ‘and-/on-’, ‘against, back’), and I render ‘turned against’, with the other reading being ‘and turned’. Beowulf says five nights against Unferth's seven (516–517) and tells the storm that Unferth left out.

sentences.t: hrēo wǣron ȳþa.
sentences.l: rough were the waves.
sentences.i: Wild were the waves.
sentences.n: ‘hrēo’ is an adjective (presumably the plural of ‘hrēoh’, ‘rough, wild, fierce’, with the final consonant lost; that is a guess at the form) in the predicate, and ‘ȳþa’ is nominative plural, ‘waves’. The clause is a half-line, and its word order (adjective, verb, noun) makes the waves the last word.

sentences.t: Wæs merefixa mōd onhrēred;
sentences.l: Was of the sea-fishes the mood stirred up;
sentences.i: The temper of the sea-beasts was stirred up;
sentences.n: ‘Wæs … onhrēred’ is a passive: ‘was stirred up’, the past participle of ‘onhrēran’ (the root of ‘rear’, as in ‘rear up’). The subject is ‘mōd’, a neuter singular, ‘mood, spirit, temper’, and ‘merefixa’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the sea-fishes’; ‘merefixa’ is ‘mere’ (sea) with the plural of ‘fisc’, and it picks up ‘hronfixas’ from 540. ‘fisc’ may cover sea-creatures in general, so this is probably the sea-monsters of 540 roused by the storm.

sentences.t:
þǣr mē wið lāðum līcsyrce mīn
heard hondlocen helpe gefremede,
beadohrægl brōden, on brēostum læg
golde gegyrwed.
sentences.l: there to me against the loathed ones my body-shirt, hard, hand-locked, help framed, the battle-garment woven, on breasts lay, adorned with gold.
sentences.i: There my mail-shirt, hard and hand-linked, gave me help against my foes — the woven war-garment that lay on my breast, adorned with gold.
sentences.n: The subject is ‘līcsyrce mīn’, ‘my body-shirt’: ‘līc’ is body and ‘syrce’ is the mail-shirt, with ‘heard hondlocen’, ‘hard, hand-locked’, as adjectives, ‘hondlocen’ being ‘hand-locked’, probably a mail-shirt whose rings were linked by hand (a guess at the exact sense). ‘helpe gefremede’ is ‘framed help’ (‘gefremman’, ‘do, perform’, with ‘helpe’, ‘help’, as its object), and ‘wið lāðum’ is ‘against the loathed ones’, dative plural, meaning the sea-beasts. ‘þǣr’ is ‘there’. The next phrases, ‘beadohrægl brōden’, ‘battle-garment woven’ (‘brōden’ is the past participle of ‘bregdan’, ‘weave, braid’, the same verb as ‘brugdon’ at 514), and ‘on brēostum læg golde gegyrwed’, ‘lay on the breast adorned with gold’, are in apposition and describe the corselet again. ‘beadohrægl’ combines ‘beadu’, battle, with ‘hrægl’, garment. The apparatus says Sievers and Holthausen would insert ‘[þæt mē]’ before ‘on brēostum’, which makes the last clause a relative clause (‘which lay on my breast’); Klaeber leaves the clauses side by side without a connecting word, and the sense is the same. ‘brēostum’ is a plural (‘on breasts’) used here of one man's chest, so the idiomatic line has the singular. Beowulf credits the corselet with helping him.

sentences.l: Me to the ground drew a hostile foe-scather; fast had me, grim, in grasp;
sentences.i: A hostile fiend dragged me to the bottom; it held me fast, grim, in its grip;
sentences.n: ‘Mē tō grunde tēah fāh fēondscaða’: ‘tēah’ is the past singular of ‘tēon’, ‘draw, drag’, with ‘mē’ as object, ‘tō grunde’ ‘to the bottom’, and ‘fāh fēondscaða’ as subject. ‘fēondscaða’ is ‘foe-scather’: ‘fēond’ is enemy or fiend, and ‘scaða’ is ‘harmer, ravager’ (cf. ‘scathe’). ‘fāh’ is a word with two meanings, ‘hostile, outlawed’ and ‘stained, coloured’ (from which comes the idea of a stained, blood-marked creature); I take the first, since it is what the context asks for, and I cannot rule out the second. In the second half ‘fæste hæfde grim on grāpe’ is ‘had fast, grim, in grasp’: the object ‘mē’ is understood from the first half, ‘grim’ is a nominative adjective on the monster, ‘fæste’ an adverb ‘firmly’ and ‘grāpe’ a dative of ‘grāp’, ‘grip, clutch’ (the root of ‘grasp’, ‘grope’).

sentences.l: yet to me it was granted that I the awesome one with point reached, with battle-blade;
sentences.i: Yet it was granted to me to reach the fearsome one with my point, with my battle-blade;
sentences.n: ‘hwæþre’ is ‘yet, nevertheless’. ‘mē gyfeþe wearð’ is ‘it was granted to me’, ‘gyfeþe’ being an adjective ‘granted, given’ in the predicate after ‘wearð’, ‘became’; the success is presented as given, not earned. The ‘þæt’-clause has ‘ic … gerǣhte’, the past subjunctive of ‘gerǣcan’, ‘reach, hit’, with ‘āglǣcan’ as its object: ‘āglǣcan’ is dative or accusative singular of ‘āglǣca’ (the weak ending is the same, so the case is not certain). This is the disputed word of Fitt II at 159, there spelled ‘ǣglǣca’; it is rendered ‘the awesome one’ in the literal line and ‘the fearsome one’ in the idiomatic, as at 424. ‘orde’ is dative singular ‘with the point’ and ‘hildebille’ is ‘with the battle-bill’, ‘bill’ being an old word for a sword blade (in apposition with ‘orde’). ‘ord’ is the point of a weapon.

sentences.t:
heaþorǣs fornam
mihtig meredēor þurh mīne hand.
sentences.l: the battle-rush carried off the mighty sea-beast through my hand.
sentences.i: and the rush of battle took the mighty sea-beast away by my hand.
sentences.n: ‘heaþorǣs’ is a masculine nominative singular, ‘battle-rush’, the subject (the same noun as ‘heaðorǣsa’ at 526, with a different spelling), and ‘fornam’ is the past of ‘forniman’, ‘take away, destroy’, with the accusative object ‘mihtig meredēor’, ‘mighty sea-deer’ (‘dēor’, wild animal, the root of ‘deer’; ‘meredēor’ is a kenning for sea-monster). ‘þurh mīne hand’ is ‘through my hand’, with the accusative after ‘þurh’. Klaeber prints no closing quotation mark, since the speech continues in the next fitt.
